chapter: Dew Drop and the name Red
title: Early gigs: stranded on the Roy Brown tour, then the Dew Drop show band
summary: He stood in for Earl Barnes on a road tour that left the band stranded in Port Arthur, then played shows at the Dew Drop.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: All right. Uh, and so when, when you got out, what, what did, uh, what did you just, did you know what you were gonna do? Now you're gonna be. No, I mean, I'm still young. I'm still young.

Mm-hmm. And I started getting a few little gigs. I don't remember what bands I played with, uh, what little gigs. There were many of them that I didn't get paid. I remember I went on the road and, uh. With who? Huh? You remember with who, who you went on the road? Uh, I know one thing. When, uh, uh, uh, what's his name, um, Good Rockin' the Night, uh. Roy Brown. Roy Brown had that record.

There was a guy that lived not too far from me. He lived on, uh, St. Anne Street off of Galvestre, but I was a guy that lived on St. Anne Street off of Galvestre. He lived on St. Anne Street off of Galvestre. By the name of, uh, Earl Barnes. Mm-hmm. Great saxophone player. He played the solo on that record. On Good Rockin' Night, yeah. So what happened, there's a promoter out of, I think, of Mississippi, or somewhere, Texas or something, that wanted to hire, see, that during that time you could, you could just put anything together. And he wanted the guy that played the solo to bring his band to the band. That was good. Uh-huh. So Earl Barnes couldn't make it. So he liked the way I played, so he sent me to be Earl Barnes. Oh, great.

The only problem was that we got stranded in, and, uh, Port Arthur, Texas. Stranded. I forgot who all was on the band. Um, it might have been, uh, uh, Lil' Dime, DuPont. August DuPont, yeah. Yeah, he, I think he might have been on it and some other guys. I don't, I can't remember, but we got stranded. And how we got home was that, uh, Earl Barnes got in touch with him and he was a Mason and he had the Masons to pay for the bus to get us back to New Orleans. He gets back home, yeah. You know. And, uh, that was one of the things that, the kind of things that were happening to me. Yeah. You know, I mean, I, you know, I didn't have a band of my own. Right. I played with whoever called me. There were times, uh, early on, that, uh, June Gardner, uh, Melvin Lasty and all of us played, went on the road, we went on the road one time. The band leader, we played at the Dew Drop, uh, and, uh, Otis Ducker had the band there. And it, Melvin Lasty, uh, August DuPont, June Gardner, and several other guys. And, uh, we, we would play, uh, the Dew Drop and do the shows and everything. That was a good experience too. And, uh, why was it, why was it a good experience? Because, uh, you, you had to play a show. You, you, you work with, with, with comedians, uh, exotic dancers, uh, singers. You had to, uh, know what cues were when they say, well, when I say something, such a thing, the bands got a hit, pop, you know, and it hit us right on our toes, you know. And we learned a lot that way, and there was certain discipline in, in playing shows. We would play the shows, and then we would play jazz or whatever we played, and take a break, and bring on a show, and go back and play jazz or whatever we were gonna do.
